questions.q: What is the core purpose of threat modeling?
options: To respond to a security incident after it has already happened
To write the final penetration test report
To think like an attacker and find weaknesses before an attack occurs
To install security tools on production servers
questions.explanation: Threat modeling is proactive: you imagine what could go wrong before an attacker ever shows up, so you can fix issues while they're still cheap to fix.

questions.q: According to the four core questions, what comes right after 'What are we building?'
options: Did we do a good job?
What can go wrong?
What are we going to do about it?
Who approved the budget?
questions.explanation: The four questions flow in order: understand the system, find what can go wrong, plan the fixes, then review whether the job was done well.

questions.q: Why does target reconstruction usually start with passive intelligence before going active?
options: Passive intelligence is always more accurate than active intelligence
Active recon is illegal in every engagement
Passive intelligence takes longer to gather
Passive methods are quiet and low-risk, letting you learn as much as possible before making noise
questions.explanation: Starting passive (job postings, OSINT) avoids detection risk, so you only go active (scans, probes) once you've extracted everything you can quietly.

questions.q: In an assumption register, what does a confidence level actually measure?
options: How much the tester wants the hypothesis to be true
How long the assumption has been in the register
How reliable the source of the observation is
How severe the vulnerability would be
questions.explanation: Confidence reflects how trustworthy the source is (e.g. client documentation vs. an inferred guess), not how exciting or desirable the finding would be.

questions.q: Why is 'absence of evidence' treated as a LOW confidence assumption?
options: Because low confidence assumptions are always wrong
Because the client documentation is never reliable
Because absence of evidence should be ignored entirely
Because not seeing proof of something is not the same as proving it is absent
questions.explanation: Never having seen a lock doesn't mean there's no lock — treating silence as proof is one of the most common mistakes in threat modeling.

questions.q: What makes an asset a 'crown jewel'?
options: It is the largest file in the system by size
It is the oldest component in the architecture
It is stored in a database rather than a file
Its loss would cause the most harm or grant an attacker the most power
questions.explanation: Crown jewels are ranked by offensive value and business harm, not by size or age — a tiny credential file can outrank a huge log archive.

questions.q: Why might a 'reachable now' asset be prioritized over a more powerful but distant one?
options: Reachable assets are always more valuable overall
Grabbing it costs little and often reveals intelligence that helps reach the deeper, primary target
Distant assets are never worth pursuing
Reachability has no effect on prioritization
questions.explanation: Reachable assets can be analyzed immediately at low cost, and often surface intelligence that makes reaching a deeper, more powerful crown jewel easier.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a policy-based and an inference-based trust boundary?
options: Inference-based boundaries are always more secure
Policy-based boundaries only exist in AI systems
Policy-based boundaries are enforced by fixed rules, while inference-based boundaries rely on the AI's changeable judgment
There is no real difference between them
questions.explanation: A policy boundary is a fixed yes/no gate (like token validation); an inference boundary depends on the model's own reasoning, which can be swayed by crafted input.

questions.q: Why is prompt injection especially dangerous against inference-based trust boundaries?
options: It attacks a boundary with no fixed rule behind it, only the model's judgment, which can be manipulated with words
Prompt injection only works against encrypted databases
It requires physical access to the server
Inference-based boundaries cannot be attacked at all
questions.explanation: Unlike a policy gate that can be picked with a stolen token, an inference gate is fooled purely with carefully crafted language.

questions.q: Where do the most dangerous escalation paths usually flow?
options: Straight through the strongest, best-defended walls
Only through the front-facing login page
Exclusively through external cloud providers
Through gaps where trust was never enforced at all
questions.explanation: Attackers rarely smash through strong defenses; they slip through boundaries where trust was assumed but never actually verified.

questions.q: Why is learning that an attack path is closed considered valuable?
options: It means the engagement has failed and should stop
It lets you stop wasting time and redirect effort toward paths that actually work
It has no value; only successful paths matter
It automatically opens three new guaranteed paths
questions.explanation: Testing a dependency gate early and finding it fails saves you from wasting hours building an attack on an assumption that was never true.

questions.q: In escalation path planning, what is a 'dependency'?
options: The final crown jewel objective
An assumption that must hold true for the path to actually work
A tool used only by defenders
The detection risk score of a path
questions.explanation: Each step in a path often depends on an unverified assumption — these dependencies act as go/no-go gates you should test before committing.

questions.q: What is the main difference between MITRE ATT&CK and MITRE ATLAS?
options: ATLAS is older and no longer used
ATT&CK covers AI attacks; ATLAS covers only cloud attacks
They are two names for the exact same catalog
ATT&CK covers traditional IT attacks; ATLAS covers AI/ML-specific attacks
questions.explanation: ATT&CK is the established catalog for general IT attacks; ATLAS is the newer catalog specifically built for attacks against AI and ML systems.

questions.q: Why does an ATLAS mapping need to evolve alongside the assumption register?
options: Because ATLAS technique IDs expire after 24 hours
Because techniques only apply once their underlying assumptions are validated, so the mapping shifts as assumptions are confirmed or dropped
Because ATLAS mappings are randomly generated
Because the mapping has no relationship to assumptions at all
questions.explanation: A technique stays 'if applicable' until its precondition assumption is validated — once validated, it becomes confirmed applicable; if invalidated, it drops off.

questions.q: What gives an intelligence brief its greatest value?
options: Its completeness — knowing every single detail
Its length — the more pages the better
Its honesty — clearly separating facts, assumptions, and constraints
Hiding uncertainty so the client feels reassured
questions.explanation: A brief's value comes from honestly distinguishing what's validated, what's assumed, and what blocks progress — not from pretending to know everything.

questions.q: Why is version history in an intelligence brief considered valuable?
options: It documents how understanding evolved over time, showing the client how uncertainty was navigated
It is only useful for billing purposes
Version history has no real value and can be discarded
It replaces the need for a risk register entirely
questions.explanation: The version history becomes a decision log — it shows not just what was found, but how the reasoning developed as new intelligence arrived.

questions.q: In the STRIDE framework, what does the 'E' stand for?
options: Encryption of data at rest
External dependency mapping
Enumeration of open ports
Elevation of Privilege — gaining more power than allowed
questions.explanation: Elevation of Privilege covers cases like a low-privilege agent invoking an admin-only tool — gaining access beyond what was intended.

questions.q: Which framework is best suited when the primary concern is data privacy specifically?
options: DREAD
LINDDUN
PASTA
STRIDE
questions.explanation: LINDDUN is STRIDE's privacy-focused cousin, purpose-built for analyzing threats to personal data specifically.

questions.q: How is the risk of a threat commonly calculated?
options: Likelihood multiplied by Impact
Impact minus Likelihood
The number of components in the system
The size of the vulnerable file
questions.explanation: Risk = Likelihood × Impact is the standard formula for prioritizing which threats to fix first, since limited time should go where it matters most.

questions.q: What does 'defense in depth' mean?
options: Relying on one very strong security control
Placing all defenses only at the network perimeter
Using multiple layers of defense so that if one fails, others still protect the system
Removing all security controls to simplify the system
questions.explanation: Defense in depth stacks several independent layers, so an attacker who defeats one control still has to get past the next one.
